title: An open agentic AI co-scientist for clinical and biomedical discovery
desc: Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer’s blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. To support research involving sensitive clinical datasets, OpenScientist can operate in a fully air-gapped environment using open-source models for inference. OpenScientist demonstrates that open, auditable, agentic AI can support real-world clinical research by researching the literature, generating hypotheses, executing analyses, and generating insights from complex datasets.

title: Interpretable AI links routine clinical gout phenotypes to multi-omic signatures and divergent health trajectories
desc: Integrative frameworks that connect scalable clinical phenotypes with molecular mechanisms are needed to resolve disease heterogeneity. We developed and externally evaluated an interpretable gout clinical-subset framework using routine data from 21,235 participants across UK Biobank (UKB; n = 10,599), the multicentre Chinese GoutRe registry (n = 8617), and MIMIC-IV (n = 2019). Unsupervised learning on six prespecified routine laboratory variables identified three subsets: C1, a low-burden state with preserved reserve; C2, a urate-metabolic inflammatory state with the greatest recurrence liability and a greater cardiometabolic and hepatic comorbidity burden; and C3, a state characterized by systemic vulnerability and higher mortality. In UKB, death-competing recurrence analysis showed a higher recurrence incidence for C2 versus C1 (subdistribution hazard ratio [sHR] 1.896, 95% CI 1.710–2.101), whereas C3 did not differ from C1 (sHR 0.994, 95% CI 0.887–1.112). A six-variable CRT model reconstructed the locked subset labels using nested 10-fold out-of-fold evaluation in UKB and external application without retraining in GoutRe and MIMIC-IV. One-versus-rest AUCs were 0.965/0.945/0.980 in UKB, 0.906/0.914/0.953 in GoutRe, and 0.912/0.898/0.962 in MIMIC-IV for C1/C2/C3, respectively. Genetic, proteomic, and metabolomic analyses supported distinct urate-inflammatory and systemic-vulnerability axes, although the C3 senescence-related genetic signal was nominal and requires replication. Routine laboratory data can identify gout clinical subsets with distinct molecular profiles and patterns of recurrence and mortality; whether these subsets can guide clinical management requires prospective evaluation.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Coronary Artery Disease: From Detection to Precision Management.
desc: [Methodist DeBakey cardiovascular journal] Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide, yet the landscape is rapidly evolving as artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to its detection, diagnosis, and management. This review surveys the expanding role of AI across the full spectrum of CAD care. In screening, deep-learning electrocardiography and electronic health record-based digital markers enable earlier identification of clinically significant disease. In noninvasive imaging, AI-driven coronary computed tomography angiography automates calcium scoring, derives fractional flow reserve without invasive wires, and quantifies high-risk plaque features that predict incident adverse events. Within the cardiac catheterization laboratory, angiography-derived physiologic assessment and AI-guided intravascular imaging segmentation support real-time procedural decision-making. Beyond diagnosis, machine-learning models integrating multimodality imaging data improve risk stratification over conventional clinical scores, while pharmacogenomic algorithms and wearable-based digital rehabilitation platforms enable patient-centric secondary prevention. Despite this progress, significant challenges persist, including limited evidence from randomized trials, algorithmic bias in underrepresented populations, regulatory uncertainty surrounding software-as-a-medical-device frameworks, and the risk of clinician de-skilling. AI has the potential to act as a collaborative tool that augments-rather than replaces-physician judgment. Future directions include foundation models, multiomics integration, agentic AI workflows, and equity-centered deployment strategies to ensure that AI-driven advances benefit all individuals with CAD.

title: Artificial Intelligence-enabled Management of Atrial Fibrillation(ABLE-AF Trial)
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Korea University Anam Hospital; conditions: AF - Atrial Fibrillation; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 1006; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common type of irregular heartbeat in adults. People with AF may also have other heart problems, including reduced heart pumping function or diseases affecting the heart muscle or heart valves. Identifying these problems early is important because the condition of the heart can affect treatment decisions and long-term care. An ultrasound examination of the heart, called transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) or an echocardiogram, is commonly used to check how well the heart pumps blood and to look for structural problems, such as heart valve disease. However, an echocardiogram requires special equipment and trained healthcare professionals to perform and interpret the examination. Because of these requirements, it may not always be available when needed. This can be particularly challenging in situations where heart function needs to be evaluated quickly, such as when a patient with AF has a very fast heart rate. Delays may also occur in outpatient settings because of limited availability of echocardiography. Artificial intelligence (AI) technology may provide an additional way to identify patients who are more likely to have heart problems and who may benefit from further evaluation. A standard 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is a simple and widely available test that records the electrical activity of the heart. AI-based computer programs can analyze information contained in an ECG that may not be easily recognized through routine interpretation. This study will use two AI-based ECG programs, called AiTiALVSD and AiTiALVDD. AiTiALVSD analyzes a standard 12-lead ECG to identify patients who may have reduced heart pumping function. Previous studies have evaluated this program in different clinical settings, including patients with AF and a fast heart rate. AiTiALVDD analyzes the ECG for signs that may be associated with difficulty in the heart relaxing and filling with blood. Problems with heart relaxation and filling may occur in several types of heart disease, including heart valve disease, abnormal thickening of the heart muscle, heart disease related to high blood pressure, diseases affecting the heart muscle, and coronary artery disease. Importantly, some patients may have these conditions even when the heart's overall pumping function is normal. title: Alloy: A Multi-Material Physics Engine for Robot Learning
desc: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU. We also report how throughput grows with the number of worlds, depth-camera throughput, agreement with closed-form references, and a reliability test over a thousand worlds.

title: Evidence-Conditioned Completion and Synthesis of Electronic Health Records
desc: Patient information can guide electronic health record (EHR) generation, but how its amount shapes predictive utility and disclosure risk remains poorly characterized. Here we present EHRDiB, which unifies visit completion and synthesis by distinguishing original missingness from withheld inputs and combining a shared multimodal representation with an evidence-conditioned latent diffusion bridge. We compared EHRDiB with three completion and eight synthesis methods on MIMIC-IV and numerical and discretized Duke Health representations. Evaluation covered downstream predictive utility, generative diversity, and distributional fidelity for both tasks, and disclosure risk for synthesis. EHRDiB achieved the smallest utility gaps from real-data-trained classifiers in seven of eight completion comparisons. In synthesis, AUPRC gaps were 45.2% smaller for ten MIMIC-IV principal-diagnosis targets and 53.3% smaller for numerical Duke Health data relative to the best comparator. Synthesis with calibrated thresholding yielded the lowest marginal distribution error across all three datasets, with Coverage above 0.95 for both output rules. Across twelve evidence-fraction intervals in MIMIC-IV synthesis, membership-inference AUROC increased from 0.516 to 0.598 as the mean target evidence fraction rose from 0.20 to 0.50; utility gaps narrowed relative to the lowest evidence configuration but did not decrease monotonically. Our study provides a unified framework and empirical foundation for EHR generation that considers both its utility for clinical analysis and its information disclosure risk.

title: Spatial causal discovery reveals novel mechanisms of cellular senescence in human liver
desc: The complex network of mechanisms that surround cellular senescence, such as its precise causes and effects, are not entirely understood at present. Senescence occurs when a cell permanently ceases dividing, halts apoptosis, stops performing its normal functions, and begins secreting chemicals that can induce other cells in its environment to also become senescent. Senescent cells are present in both healthy and unhealthy tissue, but their abundance is positively correlated with disease and age. A better understanding of senescence could lead to healthier aging, improved recovery from chemotherapy, or increased lifespan. This study used novel machine learning algorithms - with guaranteed properties of correctness under broad assumptions - to investigate senescence in human liver tissue by analyzing Visium spatial transcriptomics data. This produced data-driven models of the causes and effects of senescence, both locally and from nearby tissue. This report includes an assessment of whether the data meet key requirements for causal analysis, the transcripts identified by causal analyses as causes and effects of senescence marker genes, and pathway analyses of those gene sets.

title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
desc: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWClinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

title: Dual chain-of-thought AI‑PDCA framework for clinical history taking and documentation
desc: Clinical history-taking and documentation are foundational competencies in undergraduate medical training, yet scalable and individualized training tools remain limited. Large language model (LLM)-based systems provide automated practice opportunities but often lack structured medical reasoning, closed-loop instructional design, and integration into formal curricula. As part of a curriculum reform initiative, we constructed a clinical case repository, developed an artificial intelligence (AI)-integrated faculty Plan–Do–Check–Act (PDCA) training framework supported by dual chain-of-thought (CoT)-driven LLMs, and evaluated the reliability of AI-based scoring against faculty assessment. We then conducted a retrospective observational analysis of routinely collected educational performance data from 135 undergraduate medical students enrolled in one of three existing instructional configurations: traditional instruction, AI-assisted training, or AI + PDCA training. Educational outcomes were assessed using standardized Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) assessments. The AI + PDCA configuration was associated with the highest OSCE performance in both history-taking and clinical documentation. Among the two AI-supported configurations, longitudinal mixed-effects modeling showed steeper learning trajectories in the AI + PDCA configuration than in the AI-assisted configuration. These findings suggest that integrating AI-derived learning analytics with faculty-guided instructional intervention may support a closed-loop educational model associated with favorable competency acquisition while maintaining human oversight. This framework offers a scalable approach for implementing trustworthy, competency-based AI-enhanced medical education in routine academic practice.
